claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys maintain structural stability at high temperatures primarily because of sluggish atomic diffusion.
High-entropy nanoalloys maintain chemical stability at high temperatures primarily because of sluggish atomic diffusion.
A complex multi-element configurational landscape increases energy barriers for atomic motion.
A complex multi-element configurational landscape increases energy barriers for elemental segregation.
The as-synthesized high-entropy nanoalloy nanoparticles have a homogeneous elemental distribution.
High configurational entropy produces nanoscale grain boundaries.
High configurational entropy produces localized lattice distortions.
The presence of multiple principal elements creates a complex local energy landscape.
The complex local energy landscape significantly impedes atomic mobility.
Impeded atomic mobility reduces the rate of phase separation during high-temperature exposure.
Impeded atomic mobility reduces grain-growth rates during high-temperature exposure.
Impeded atomic mobility reduces chemical segregation during high-temperature exposure.
High-entropy nanoalloys will have lower atomic diffusion coefficients than simpler nanoalloys or bulk-alloy baselines under identical high-temperature conditions.
High-entropy nanoalloys will show a delayed onset of phase transformations relative to simpler nanoalloys or bulk-alloy baselines under identical high-temperature conditions.
High-entropy nanoalloys will undergo less grain growth than simpler nanoalloys or bulk-alloy baselines under identical high-temperature conditions.
The predicted stability advantage depends on retention of high configurational entropy.
Strongly oxidizing atmospheres, high thermal gradients, or significant composition deviations may alter the predicted stability advantage.
